meaningMnemonic: This radical is the same as the kanji. It means name .
Inside this guy's forehead you have a spoon and a bunch of hair, not to mention whatever that is in the top left. That's the mind of a psychopath right there.

Although a little bit modified, there is a turtle shell that's on a mustache with this radical. The only thing with a mustache that hangs around turtles is Splinter, the giant rat from Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. So this radical is Splinter (the giant rat).

The leader , Master Splinter (the rat from Ninja Turtles) isn't even supposed to exist. He exists because someone accidentally poured ooze on him. Hints Imagine someone accidentally spilling ooze on a rat, then watch the rat turn into a sentient rat martial artist.
readingMnemonic: But really, if you do something accidentally , it's probably a goo d ( ぐう ) thing in a way. You learn a bit about how you can improve yourself so you don't do it again, or in Splinter's case, it's just a good mistake! Hints However you look at it, try to make this accident be a good accident.

meaningMnemonic: The construction of an under ground prison will be done by someone who is adept at it. Hints And that adept person is you! You're an expert when it comes to constructing underground prisons, so you've been hired for this job. Good luck!
readingMnemonic: Adept at constructing underground prisons, you've caught the eye of Emperor こう いち , the royal underground prison enthusiast. Hints With a dignified nod, Emperor こういち entrusts you with the grand project of constructing an underground prison, confident that the adept builder will make prisoners feel right at home in their new subterranean digs. Hint: When you see 工 in a kanji it will often take the こう reading.

meaningMnemonic: A fish with two mouth s has the number two on it because it's in prison (that's its prison number). Who put the poor two-mouthed fish in prison? An alligator . Because alligators hate two-mouthed fish. Hints How the alligator wishes it had a second mouth like the fish with two mouths, prisoner number 2! It believes that with another mouth, it would be the most talked-about predator, so it imprisons the two-mouthed fish out of jealousy.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the わに in "WaniKani." Ever heard of it? Hints So long as you've ever used WaniKani, you probably know the reading of the word alligator.

meaningMnemonic: Why would you put your fingers on a bed ? To bundle up the sheets — maybe because you need to do laundry or something. Grasp that bundle of sheets tightly, and be careful not to let it unfurl as you carry it on over to the washing machine. Hints Imagine pressing your fingers into the bed, grasping tightly and ripping the sheets free. Now bundle them up, tight as you can!
readingMnemonic: As you bundle up your sheets and grasp them tightly, you triumphantly exclaim, " Hah ( は )!" to all your imaginary naysayers. In your mind, everyone doubted that you could actually bundle up your own sheets and launder them yourself. Hints Hah! Take that naysayers! Who's bundling their own sheets now? Me, that's who! Hah!

meaningMnemonic: A horse that is fat is a burdensome animal. Hints A fat horse. So burdensome. Not to mention the burden on the horse on top of the fatness.
readingMnemonic: But you have to be nice to the burdensome horse because this horse is your da d ( だ ). Hints Go visit your dad the burdensome horse because you have to visit your dad. It's weird because you're a human and he's a horse.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami is the same as a cave . Because, if a wave is big enough, it will curl over on itself, creating a sort of cave within the wave. That's why it's the same as a cave! Hints Also, imagine a tsunami hitting a cave, becoming the same as the cave (since a cave will shape it).
readingMnemonic: Best way to remember the reading for this kanji is to think about how the shape of a cave is the shape of a dou ghnut ( どう ). Hints Also note that the 同 part of this kanji gives away the reading as well. 同 and 洞 have the same readings!

meaningMnemonic: The leader all in white is the chief . All the other leaders are wearing some other color, but that's how you tell the chief apart from the other leaders. Hints Imagine all the leaders standing around, then the chief person standing there all in white.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as 白 , which is included in this kanji. The other reading is お , and it's like the honorific 御 , in a way. You'd want to be polite to someone who is the chief ______, right? That's why it could be お , too. Hints You'll learn more about which reading to use when the vocabulary roll around. In the meantime, try to remember both of them the best you can!

meaningMnemonic: Under a canopy held up by a stick , Wolverine opens his mouth and says, " China !" Why would he say China? It's all very sudden . Hints Picture Wolverine shouting "China!" in his canopy all of a sudden. Okay, he only said "China" because someone asked him to name a country, and when he looked at his canopy, it reminded him of a pagoda.
readingMnemonic: This sudden urge to shout " China " also came about because Wolverine woke up in とう きょう . Outside of his pagoda-shaped canopy, Wolverine noticed the kanji and assumed he was in China. Hints Imagine scowling at Wolverine for getting China and とうきょう mixed up. In his defense, he hasn't been learning Japanese like you have, so you can forgive him. He should really do better though.

meaningMnemonic: You want to write a chapter about hair in your new book so you have to make sure it's really clear . Clear enough so that ANYbody can read it. Hints Your writing is so clear and concise that just about everyone does read it. Well, everyone with hair that is.
readingMnemonic: Your clear writing got the attention of the Shou gun ( しょう ) and now he's at your door once again. Although, this time he's angrier than usual. His hair also looks awful. He took your advice after reading the book and cut his entire ponytail off. Hints Picture the Shougun angrily yelling at you about his hair disaster! The only good thing he can say about your book is that it gave clear directions.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami crashes into the sun , which is then caught in a net and tied to a stool ! Wait a second... this doesn't sound realistic, it sounds really comic ! That's because it's from that comic book about a pirate you're always reading! Hints Imagine reading this issue of your favorite stretchy pirate boy comic. Lumpy uses his long arms as a net, traps the sun and ties it to the stool right as the tsunami hits. What kind of crazy trouble is he getting into this time?!
readingMnemonic: Comic s are man ga ( まん ) in Japan, whether they're comic or serious. Hints You've known about Japanese comics or manga for a long time, and now you can read them too. Look how far you've come. Wow, what a journey. I'm just so proud of you, kiddo.

meaningMnemonic: Watch what you say next from your mouth when someone comes to consult with you. Hints This person wants to consult you about something important, so whatever you say next from your mouth better be really smart-sounding and helpful. Make this person glad they consulted you.
readingMnemonic: After they consult with you, the person decides to buy a shee p ( し ). Hints They were on the fence about buying one, which is why they consulted with you. You think sheep are the ultimate safe-haven asset, so you told them not to be sheepish and advised them to invest in one.

meaningMnemonic: The Yoga King presides over all courts : law, imperial, and so forth. In this case, you've met him in the court of law, where he is judge, jury, and executioner. Hints Picture him sitting above you in the judge's chair in court. He's about to make his judgement.
readingMnemonic: The court of the Yoga King is against you. You have to turn this around, so you start pushing ta ter ( てい ) tots into his tater-tot-hole shaped mouth. Hints "I hereby sentence you to..." *ploop* "Ooh, this is really good. I hereby sentence..." *ploop* "Wow, are these tater tots? Court dismissed."

meaningMnemonic: This is an animal with an angle d sword claw that's filled with cow meat but looks like an insect . What kind of animal is that? It's a crab . Hints If you think about the different parts you can see why this is a crab. A delicious, delicious crab.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the かに in WaniKani. Hints If you've used WaniKani before, you probably know this reading, hopefully. All praise the great allicrab!

meaningMnemonic: A woman is making a dirt cage in the sun . She's using it to trap water, making this a dirt dam . If you think about it, dams are just dirt cages anyway. Hints Picture the woman working tirelessly in the hot sun, moving and shaping the dirt around this river into a dam to make a pond.
readingMnemonic: Something about the woman working hard to build this dam makes her super sexy ( せき ) to you. Maybe it's because the sun is so bright, making her shine, or maybe it's because hard work is attractive. Who knows. Hints If you wanna be sexy maybe you should build a dam too.

meaningMnemonic: If a tsunami hits your helicopter while you are jackhammer ing, it will drift out to sea. What were you doing with a jackhammer at a time like this? Now your helicopter is drifting away! Hints Picture your helicopter as it drifts out to sea with the tsunami.
readingMnemonic: As it drift s away you shout, " Heyooo ! ( ひょう )." You know the helicopter probably can't hear you (or understand you) but maybe it will turn on and stop drifting away if you shout it enough. Hints "Heyoooo stop drifting awaaaay!!"

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami slams through your roof and smashes your coat rack , creating a swirling eddy where it used to be. Hints An eddy requires water to change direction and then twirl around, and somehow the force of the tsunami hitting your coat rack caused one to form. That's science for you, I guess.
readingMnemonic: As you stare at the swirling eddy , you're suddenly overtaken by the urge to yodel ( よど ). Something about the eddy's crystalline purity reminds you of the water in the Swiss Alps, and that really puts you in the mood to yodel. Hints Imagine pulling on some lederhosen and yodeling your heart out beside the churning eddy in your closet. It's quite an idyllic sight.

meaningMnemonic: Take some dirt , let it harden in the sun , then pile it up around a coat rack to create a nice embankment . Every embankment secretly has a coat rack holding up all its sun-hardened dirt. Didn't you know? Hints Feel the sun beating down on your tired limbs as you pack this dirt around the base of a coat rack. The coat rack provides structure and makes the embankment nice and strong.
readingMnemonic: The secret to building a good embankment is ta ter ( てい ) tots. You gotta mix those taters in with the dirt as you pile it up around the coat rack. The taters give the embankment the springy elasticity and spongy absorbency necessary to keep raging flood waters in check. Hints You can also snack on the tater tots while constructing your embankment, which is nice. Just take care to keep your taters clearly separate from your other materials, or else you might get confused and accidentally eat a handful of dirt or something.

meaningMnemonic: You walk out on a cliff , where you find in the ground a mouth poking out. It speaks: "It is me, the empress of these lands!" Hints She was buried in the cliff down to her mouth so nobody would find her! You pull her out of the ground and soon what was just a mouth becomes a whole empress!
readingMnemonic: When you finish unburying the empress , the first thing she says to you is: "Please, you must hurry and take me to Emperor こう いち ." Hints It's only natural the empress would want to see her emperor. And right now, the emperor of these lands is Emperor こういち .

meaningMnemonic: Turn a sick ness into a weapon and it becomes an epidemic . This sickness spreads to everyone and it's all your fault because you put it in the water supply. Hints Imagine if countries decided to make sick weapons that would spread epidemics like this all over part of the world. Let's hope they don't...
readingMnemonic: These epidemic s spread by 駅 ( えき ). Each train takes the sickness and shoots off in a different direction, spreading it further. Hints Picture a single 駅 on a map, bright red. Now watch the red spread to all of the other 駅 on the map, dyeing them red and spreading the epidemic all over your country.

meaningMnemonic: You have a number ed feather . Pick your favorite number and put it on the feather. Then, put the numbered feather on your head. When you put it on, you're able to flip and flip over and over. Hints Imagine yourself doing flips with this feather on your head. Flip flip flip.
readingMnemonic: You're pretty good at your flip technique, but you're not that good. You really need to practice and hone ( ほん ) your skills and get better. Hints Or, maybe you get so good that you write a 本 ( ほん ) about doing a flip. Wow, you're good!

meaningMnemonic: A tree can be a tree , but it can also be a psychopath . The tree goes from being a regular tree to being a psychopath. Such mood swings are so rough. Especially when the tree slips to gloom . Hints Imagine all the mood swings of this tree. Psychopath tree! Also very gloomy sometimes.
readingMnemonic: Then the tree switches from gloom to being super excited (these moodswings!). The super excited tree starts doing dubstep. Uts ( うつ ) uts uts uts uts ♬. Hints Sing along with the moody tree. Gloom to dubstep. Such a big change.

meaningMnemonic: There is a tsunami coming up over a cliff made of dirt . You can see this happening very far away because it's right on the horizon . Hints Picture the tsunami breaking over the cliff on the horizon. It would be beautiful if it wasn't so frightening.
readingMnemonic: You squint into the horizon and see something else. There's some guy ( がい ) up there. And he's... he's being swept away by the tsunami. The guy disappears into the horizon. The guy is gone. Hints You wonder who that guy was. You wonder why he was there. You wonder if he's still alive out there, past the horizon.

meaningMnemonic: A gold name on this piece of wood is the inscription that shows the artist's signature. Hints This inscription refers to a signature or something similar. This is an artisan's signature in the form of an inscription.
readingMnemonic: The inscription is a name written on something, right? Remember the kanji for "name"? It is 名 , and it shares the reading with this kanji as well, making both names めい . Hints If you need to review 名 go ahead and do that. It will help you to remember this kanji.

meaningMnemonic: The leader cat pirate is the greatest cat pirate of them all. It leads all the cat pirate leaders, even! This is truly a cat pirate to look up to . Hints Imagine this majestic cat pirate leader of leaders. Feel in your heart that you look up to this cat pirate, truly.
readingMnemonic: Your job is to bring this leader of cat pirates (whom you look up to ) its favorite food: gyo za ( ぎょう ). Hints Of course, the gyoza is filled with fish, because we're talking about cat pirates, here.

meaningMnemonic: Why would a samurai go to mainland Asia ? To buy a pot , of course! Asia's full of potters making all kinds of cool traditional pots and jar s. The samurai probably wants to take them back home and show them off to his pot-loving samurai buddies. Hints Picture a lone samurai — like a ronin or something — wandering the pottery markets of mainland Asia in search of beautiful pots and jars to take back to Japan. What a cultured guy.
readingMnemonic: Specifically, this samurai wants to buy a pot big enough to hold two bo dies ( つぼ ). Why? Well, samurai have a lot of enemies. I wouldn't pry into it too much — you might end up as one of the two bodies inside the pot. Hints Imagine this samurai walking around a pottery market asking vendors about pots and jars "big enough for two bodies." Everyone's getting pretty sketched out.

meaningMnemonic: A bamboo tsunami uses its drop s to carry out its specialty , which is turning itself into record book s. Hints The bamboo tsunami hits the ground and drops of bamboo turn into sheets of paper. The sheets of paper combine to become record books that record what happened here, on this day.
readingMnemonic: A record book is a bo ok ( ぼ ), when it comes down to it. Hints Bamboo can also become bo staffs too, if they don't turn into record books.

meaningMnemonic: The restaurant radical and the restaurant kanji are the same! The meaning of this kanji also extends other resting places, like an inn or a pavilion . Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: This restaurant only serves tater ( てい ) tots. Really, would you ever want to go to a restaurant that didn't have tater tots? No. Hints Imagine going to a restaurant and seeing a menu of all different types and styles of tater tots and nothing else. Even the drinks are tater tot based. Mmm mm.

meaningMnemonic: What you say on the street needs to be revise d. Your words need to be polished, you can't publish improv. Revise your street word inspiration before you share it again. Hints Think about all the stupid things you said on the streets today. Do you want those exact phrases, mistakes, and mouth sounds following you around forever? Revise it before you write it down!
readingMnemonic: You want to revise the song you wrote about ta ter ( てい ) tots at lunch today. But it needs a lot of revising. Hints "Tater tots, tater tots, tater tots, man. Bake me a tater tot as fast as you banana." Well that's bad. Better revise this so it rhymes. "Tater tots, tater tots, tater tots, man. Bake me a tater tot as fast as you want." Nope, still bad. Revise! "Tater tots, tater tots, tater tots, man. Bake me a tater tot as fast as you clam." Yes. It's gold.

meaningMnemonic: A samurai who can fight with icicle s on him is more robust than regular samurai. Can you imagine how robust you'd have to be to fight in weather cold enough to form icicles on your body? Hints Picture samurai standing in a line. One, two, three... woah. You look up. This guy has icicles growing off him and he's the size of a bus. Now that's a robust samurai.
readingMnemonic: You may think it's just his robust body, but it's actually the samurai's robust sou l ( そう ) that keeps him fighting through the cold and the icicles. Hints Physical robustness is just a reflection of the strength of your soul!

meaningMnemonic: There are nine car s all driving in the same place. With so many cars driving in the same place, they create a rut . Hints Imagine the cars spinning out in the rut. Spin spin spin. The rut gets bigger. Nine is too many cars.
readingMnemonic: To get out of the rut you have to put in a second key ( き ) that turns on the thrusters. You put in the key and press the "take off" button. Hints Imagine turning the thrusters key, then feeling the car lift off the ground. You'll finally get out of this rut !

meaningMnemonic: A big turkey in the rice paddy is getting all stirred up . He's kicking up all the rice. Who stirred him up? Hints He is a really big turkey too. Like, 12 feet tall, or something. Don't want to stir up a turkey that's that big.
readingMnemonic: While the turkey is stirred up , it also looks like it's having a lot of fun ( ふん ). Hints Is it laughing? Oh no, this is bad, it's enjoying being stirred up, now we'll never stop it.

meaningMnemonic: At the top of the mountain is a signpost to tell you you've reached the summit . Literally every mountain that humans have reached the top of has one of these summit signs. Hints If that signpost wasn't there how would you know you reached the summit? Like, if you were on top of Everest and there was a bad storm... you'd just topple off the other side. Those summit signposts are important!
readingMnemonic: At the summit , you decide to build your new ho me ( ほう ). It's been destroyed so many times, and you're sick of it. Maybe if you build your home at the summit of this mountain it will be safer. Hints Picture your beautiful summit home. You know, George Washington had one of these too. So. That's cool, I guess.

meaningMnemonic: Sticking out of the dirt , there's a cross adorned with flowers and shellfish shells. This is a tomb . The flowers and shellfish were put here as decorations and to honor the dead that currently lie under the dirt. And the cross marks the tomb, obviously. Hints Can you picture this big dirt tomb, with flowers and shellfish decorating it and a cross right on top?
readingMnemonic: This is a tomb , but it feels really fun ( ふん ). Decorated with flowers and shellfish shells, it’s not a sad place at all. It's a fun place to remember all the fun times with people you loved. Hints See this tomb, and you'll remember all the fun you had. It's decorated to make sure you feel that fun. Fun fact: when you see 賁 in a kanji, the reading is probably going to be ふん .

meaningMnemonic: With your fingers you put some weapon s in a boat for transport . This is a transport boat and its your job to get these weapons from one place to another. Hints Imagine loading a bunch of weapons into a boat and sailing off to transport them somewhere else.
readingMnemonic: Hey! You're transport ing weapons just like Han ( はん ) Solo! I mean, it was a spaceship, not technically a boat, but he definitely used the Millennium Falcon as a transport. Hints Picture yourself as a cool smuggler, transporting stolen... I mean... totally legitimate weapons from one place to another. Just like Han Solo!

meaningMnemonic: A fang on a building shows that it's wicked . Something wicked probably lives in the building too. Hints Not like, wicked cool, but like wicked evil. I see you, New Englanders.
readingMnemonic: You peek inside the wicked building and a wicked ja guar ( じゃ ) suddenly pounces at you! You let out a sigh of relief when it's stopped by the window, but then... the window opens?! What a wicked building! It's letting the jaguar get you! Hints Imagine being chased around the outside of this wicked fanged building as the wicked fanged jaguar tries to eat you. Ahhh!

meaningMnemonic: A sudden stab is abrupt and unexpected . Quick, dodge!! 唐突 describes sudden actions or events that catch people off guard.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 彼女、唐突に車の修理をしてほしいって俺に頼んできたんだよ。
sentences.english: She suddenly asked me to repair her car.

meaningMnemonic: A notebook that is also a record book is an account book or register , showing the records of all the transactions that have gone through.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 帳簿を燃やしてしまうという考えは思いつきませんでした。
sentences.english: I didn’t think of the idea to burn the account book.

meaningMnemonic: You're so adept ! That makes you adept at that thing. Skillful and clever are other ways to do it too.
readingMnemonic: Remember 旨い , which means "delicious"? Remember how it also means "skillful" and "clever"? It's the same with this word, and the reading is the same as well.

sentences.japanese: 話が巧すぎるぜ。何か企んでるだろ？
sentences.english: It’s too good to be true. What are you scheming?

meaningMnemonic: The great alligator ! This can mean both alligator or crocodile , because really, they're not so different, are they? No crabigator, that's for sure.
readingMnemonic: The reading is a reading you've known your whole life. It's like you were born with the reading, whispering in your ear, ready to emerge at just the right moment... and that moment is now.

sentences.japanese: この鰐の置物、邪魔なんだけど。
sentences.english: This alligator statue is in the way.

sentences.japanese: 鰐蟹って漢字、何も見ずに手書きで書けるの？すごいね！
sentences.english: You can handwrite the kanji for WaniKani without looking at anything? That's amazing!

sentences.japanese: 鰐の剥製が部屋に飾ってあります。
sentences.english: I have a stuffed alligator displayed in my room.

meaningMnemonic: An old tomb is an ancient tomb . They're mostly from the Kofun period, and indeed that's where the period gets its name.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 近年その古墳を訪れる人が増えています。
sentences.english: The number of people visiting the ancient tomb has been increasing in recent years.

sentences.japanese: このカフェでは、古墳の形をしたケーキが食べれます。
sentences.english: In this cafe, you can eat cakes in the shape of ancient tombs.

sentences.japanese: 古川君は、古墳マニアなんですよ。
sentences.english: Furukawa-kun is ancient tomb enthusiast.

sentences.japanese: 古墳時代は、三世紀末頃から七世紀頃までの時代を言います。
sentences.english: The Kofun period refers to the period from around the end of the 3rd century to the 7th century.

meaningMnemonic: Who is the chief mother ? That's your aunt . And this aunt is the older sister of your mom or dad because she is the chief mother. An aunt who is a younger sister of your parent is 叔母 , which is another word for "aunt" you already know!
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is an exception. But you already learned the 叔母 which means aunt too. Well they have the same reading! So if you know one aunt, you know them all.

sentences.japanese: 伯母はどうして私達の結婚式に来ようとしなかったんだろう。
sentences.english: I wonder why my aunt didn’t come to our wedding ceremony.

meaningMnemonic: The inscription 's pattern shows what brand or make this item is. If the pattern of the inscription is an apple, you'll know the brand is Apple. If it's a Window, you know it's Microsoft. Etc.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the on'yomi reading for the first kanji and the kun'yomi reading for the second. Luckily, you've learned them both already so you should be able to slap them together and know the reading of this word!

sentences.japanese: 後どれくらいでお客さんに推奨する銘柄が決まりそうですか。
sentences.english: How much longer will it take you to decide which brand to recommend to your customer?

meaningMnemonic: Something that happened accidentally by nature probably happened by chance or unexpectedly . It was just a coincidence !
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 偶然の一致に思わず笑ってしまった。
sentences.english: I couldn't help but laugh at the coincidence.

sentences.japanese: 偶然なショットだけど、いい写真が撮れた。
sentences.english: It was an accidental shot, but it turned out to be a good photo.

sentences.japanese: 空港で偶然、高校時代の友人に会ったんですよ。
sentences.english: I unexpectedly ran into a friend from high school at the airport.

meaningMnemonic: Transport and exit these goods from here (by transporting them). Take it away. It's time to carry out .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 日曜の夜七時までに全ての作品を搬出する必要があります。
sentences.english: By 7pm on Sunday, we need to take out all of our work pieces.

meaningMnemonic: A horse riding soldier is a member of the cavalry .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: その騎兵の写真、なんだか若かりし頃を思い出すな。
sentences.english: That photo of the cavalries reminds me a bit of my youth.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: Hoe Ra ( ほら ), the version of Ra who carries a hoe around, is using said hoe to dig out a cave for himself, to provide shade from the sun (despite being the god of sun). He digs digs digs and then sits in his nice cave, hoe in hand.

sentences.japanese: その薄気味悪い洞は、村の北外れにひっそりとたたずんでいました。
sentences.english: The eerie cave stood silently on the village's northern outskirts.

meaningMnemonic: A cave hole is a cave or den .
readingMnemonic: The reading of 洞 is one you've learned. The reading of 穴 isn't one you've learned, though. So, think about how you go inside this cave , only to find yourself covered by some red goopy liquid. You think it's blood, but luckily it just turns out to be ketsu p ( けつ ). If you want to be less formal, you can also use the kun'yomi and say ほらあな , but then you'd never learn that reading for 穴 , and where's the fun in that?

sentences.japanese: その洞穴でつまずいて、足首を捻挫しました。
sentences.english: I stumbled in the cave and sprained my ankle.

meaningMnemonic: When you flip your idea of something, you're changing how you think about it. That's why this word is change one's mind .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: この結婚について、絶対に翻意することがないことを誓います。
sentences.english: I swear, I will absolutely not change my mind about this marriage.

meaningMnemonic: The chief of this district is that guy, the count . He's also the earl of another district, and the chief of yet another.
readingMnemonic: The reading is the はく reading you learned with the kanji.

meaningMnemonic: A public announcement is a public notice . 公告 looks and sounds a lot like 広告 , but the meanings are different. You might remember 広告 is for advertisements, but 公告 here is for the kind of official statements that companies or governments put out for the public, especially shareholders, creditors, or other stakeholders. You can remember 公告 is a public notice because the kanji for "public" is 公 , and it's not covered by a canopy like the other one. It's uncovered, all out in the open for everyone to see — public!
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: トーフグの決算公告、もう見ましたか。
sentences.english: Did you already see Tofugu's public, financial announcement?

sentences.japanese: 私はそのダイヤモンドの輝きに目がくらんでしまいました。
sentences.english: I was disoriented by the radiance of the diamond.

readingMnemonic: The reading comes from the word 殴る and the kanji 込 .

sentences.japanese: 殴り込みの前に早めの昼食を取りました。
sentences.english: We had an early lunch before the raid.

Go ahead and walk around your room and feel this rhythm. Note that リズム is a much more common word to use for "rhythm," but you may see the kanji version sometimes in formal writing. One thing you will see more often is 律動的 which means "rhythmic."
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned 煮る , which is used for when you purposefully boil something. This verb, on the other hand, is intransitive, meaning that it refers to when something is getting boiled or cooked up, with no emphasis on who put the thing in the pot. That's why this verb means to be boiled or to be cooked .

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. While the kanji means flip , the verb vocab version is to billow or to flutter , as in some kind of material (maybe a dress or a flag) billowing or fluttering in the wind. It can also mean to suddenly change your mind, or your attitude, etc.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means consult and the verb vocab version is to consult with or to confer with . 諮る is a very formal word that refers to consulting someone for advice or approval — usually a group, council, or authority. You'll see it in political or business contexts, like 計画を審議会に諮る (to submit a plan to the committee for consideration).
readingMnemonic: You need to consult with a hacker ( はか ) to solve your hacking problem. Imagine what kind of hacking problem you need to discuss, then imagine consulting with a hacker — whatever a hacker looks like in your mind.

sentences.japanese: この問題は取締役会に諮る必要があります。
sentences.english: We need to discuss this problem at the board of directors meeting.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means drift and the verb vocab version is to drift or to waft .

meaningMnemonic: 尽きる is "to be exhausted." 尽くす is when you're doing the exhausting of something, which makes it to exhaust something . You'll also see 尽くす attached to other verbs to mean to do fully , like 使い尽くす (to use up completely) or 焼き尽くす (to burn to ashes).

meaningMnemonic: You know that 雪崩 is "avalanche" and that the 込 kanji means into . readingMnemonic: This word uses the readings you learned with the kanji, so you should be all set. Just be careful with 雪崩 , since the れ in なだれ is sticking out of the kanji.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. Notice how it shares its reading with 蓄える and its kanji with 貯める ? It also has a similar meaning — to set aside . Note that 貯える is less common in modern writing, and often feels a little old-fashioned. But you might still see it in contexts where it means to store up food and supplies for future needs (like 蓄える ) or to save up money (like 貯める ).
readingMnemonic: This shares a reading with 蓄える , which makes sense since their meanings are so similar! Here's a mnemonic just in case you don't remember the reading: You need to set aside some things, so you take one ( たくわ ) and set it aside, then take one more and set it aside again. Repeat this process to store up lots of things over time.

meaningMnemonic: Here, 歳 means year and 暮 comes from 暮れる (to end). So 歳暮 literally means "end of the year," but in modern Japanese, this almost always refers to a year-end gift , which is basically a way to say thanks before the year wraps up. 歳暮 is almost always used with the honorific お , as in お歳暮 . It's a formal gift, like nicely-wrapped boxed sweets or coffee sent to bosses, clients, or people who have helped you during the year.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You haven't learned this reading for 歳 yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out: There's one year-end gift that always makes people happy: a sa ber ( せい ). Who wouldn't be stoked to get a saber as an end-of-year gift? It might be a little tricky to wrap, though…
